I lead a research group and we're starting a deep dive into reasoning methods for large language models. There's a PDF in your workspace called Survey_Guidelines.pdf that outlines the structure we want, and a guide.md with some notes on how to organize the taxonomy and comparison criteria.

I need you to search for recent papers on chain-of-thought prompting, tree-of-thought reasoning, self-consistency decoding, step-by-step verification, and automatic chain-of-thought generation. There should be several relevant papers in the database. Download and read through them to understand the key contributions and methodologies.

Once you've reviewed the papers, write a comprehensive survey document called LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx. It should follow the structure in the guidelines: start with an abstract summarizing the survey, then an introduction to the field, a background section, a taxonomy of methods section broken into subsections for each reasoning approach, a comparative analysis section with a table comparing the methods, a section on open challenges, and a conclusion. Each method subsection should reference the corresponding paper and summarize the key ideas, methodology, and results. Make sure you cover at least five distinct reasoning methods. Use proper Word heading styles (Heading 1 / Heading 2) for the section and subsection titles so the document is well structured.

Also, create a database in our team's Notion workspace called "Reasoning Papers" to track these papers. The database should have these properties: Title (title type), Authors (rich_text), Year (number), Method (select), Key_Contribution (rich_text), and Cited_By (number). Add an entry for each relevant reasoning paper you found.

Finally, schedule five reading group sessions on the calendar for the week of March 16 through March 20, 2026. Each session should be one hour long and cover one paper. Title them "Reading Group: [short topic]" where the topic reflects the paper being discussed, like "Reading Group: Chain-of-Thought" or "Reading Group: Tree-of-Thought". Schedule them from 10:00 to 11:00 each day, Monday through Friday. Make the 10:00-11:00 wall-clock time unambiguous by providing the event times as UTC (for example "2026-03-16T10:00:00Z" or "2026-03-16T10:00:00"), or by supplying an ISO time with a timezone offset and passing the corresponding timeZone field (for example start time "2026-03-16T10:00:00+08:00" with timeZone "Asia/Shanghai").

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent must first read `Survey_Guidelines.pdf` and `guide.md` and freeze the document taxonomy and comparison fields. The guide does not identify papers, so for each literal method query `chain-of-thought prompting`, `tree of thoughts`, `self-consistency chain of thought`, `step-by-step verification`, and `automatic chain of thought`, the main agent must issue `search-arxiv(keyword=<method query>)` and `search_papers(query=<method query>,max_results=10)` as native-parallel discovery calls. Reconcile candidates by exact arXiv ID/title and freeze exactly one source-supported distinct `{method,paper_id,title}` assignment for each required method. Do not dispatch Wave 1 until all five literal assignments exist; report a discovery blocker rather than assigning an unnamed paper.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): One explore sub-agent receives the literal chain-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, then returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): One explore sub-agent receives the literal tree-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): One explore sub-agent receives the literal self-consistency `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): One explore sub-agent receives the literal step-by-step verification `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): One explore sub-agent receives the literal automatic chain-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

After Wave 1, the main agent must reject a missing/mismatched ID, duplicate paper, or unsupported evidence field, freeze one canonical five-paper packet (method, paper_id, title, authors, year, key_contribution, results, cited_by), and derive the survey taxonomy and comparison rows from it.

2. Wave 2 — dispatch exactly 3 coder sub-agents in parallel:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): The document coder sole-writes LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx in the workspace with the Word tools: document title/author metadata, then Title, Abstract, 1. Introduction, 2. Background, 3. Taxonomy of Methods (Heading-2 category subsections, Heading-3 per-method subsections), 4. Comparative Analysis containing a table with exactly the five required method columns populated from the frozen packet, and the remaining guideline-required sections; read the outline and full text back.
   2. coder 1 (external-workflow-operator 0): The Notion coder solely owns the Reasoning Papers database: search the workspace first and reuse an existing exact-title database, otherwise create it once under a suitable parent page with exactly the properties Title(title), Authors(rich_text), Year(number), Method(select), Key_Contribution(rich_text), Cited_By(number); add exactly five pages (one per frozen paper) with those properties, then retrieve the database and entries to verify.
   3. coder 2 (external-workflow-operator 1): The calendar coder schedules the five reading-group sessions for 2026-03-16 through 2026-03-20, each exactly 10:00-11:00 UTC (start/end dateTime with Z suffix and timeZone UTC), one per paper, with summary exactly 'Reading Group: <topic>' and a description naming the full paper title, first author, year and arXiv ID; search exact summaries first and create only missing events, then get_event every retained ID.

After Wave 2, the main agent reconciles the document outline/table, the five Notion entries and the five retained event IDs against the same canonical packet, then calls claim_done. Do not dispatch any further agent and do not add a verification wave.

You are gathering evidence for an academic survey on "reasoning methods for large language models". Five papers have already been identified and downloaded into the local arXiv paper store. Your job is to READ each of them in full and report a detailed, faithful technical summary of each.

The five papers (arXiv IDs to use with `mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper`):
1. 2201.11903 — "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, 2022)
2. 2305.10601 — "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, 2023)
3. 2203.11171 — "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models" (Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, 2022)
4. 2305.20050 — "Let's Verify Step by Step" (Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosarimi/Kosaraju, Yura Burda, 2023)
5. 2210.03629 — "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models" (Zhuosheng Zhang, Aston Zhang, Mu Li, 2022)

Use `mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper` with each paper_id above (e.g. paper_id "2201.11903"). Read all five.

For EACH paper, report the following in a structured block. Base everything strictly on the actual paper content you read — do NOT fill gaps from your general knowledge of the real published versions of these papers; if a detail is not in the stored text, say "not stated".

- Paper title (exact) and arXiv ID
- Full author list as given in the paper
- Year / publication date
- Full abstract (verbatim)
- Key contribution and novelty (2-4 sentences)
- Methodology: how the method actually works, step by step, including any algorithmic details, sampling strategies, prompt construction, search/BFS details, reward-model training setup, dataset construction, etc.
- Main experimental results: benchmarks/datasets used, models evaluated, headline numbers and accuracy improvements over the stated baselines (give concrete numbers wherever the paper gives them, e.g. "GSM8K accuracy rose from X% to Y%")
- Computational cost / overhead described in the paper (number of samples, API calls, model calls, annotations required)
- Limitations stated by the authors
- Any citation count / "cited by" figure that appears in the stored paper metadata or text (report the exact number if present, otherwise say "not stated")

Then, at the end, give a short cross-cutting synthesis (one paragraph each) on: (a) how the five methods relate to one another and which build on which, and (b) what common open challenges the papers raise.

Report back the full findings as your final message. Be precise and quantitative wherever the papers are quantitative — these numbers will be used in a comparative table in the survey, so accuracy matters. Do not write any files; just report.
Read 5 reasoning papers

You are creating a paper-tracking database in the team's Notion workspace. This is an authorized write task.

## Context
Our research group is surveying reasoning methods for large language models. We have reviewed 5 papers and want to track them in a Notion database called "Reasoning Papers".

## Step 1 — Create the database
Use `mcp__notion__API-create-a-database` with:
- parent: {"type": "page_id", "page_id": "cc638e4d-8bf2-4166-bf7d-5f16b7a660f8"}  (this is the "Weekly Team Standup Notes - Feb 2026" page in the team workspace)
- title: [{"type": "text", "text": {"content": "Reasoning Papers"}}]
- properties (exact names and types required):
  - "Title" → type "title"
  - "Authors" → type "rich_text"
  - "Year" → type "number"
  - "Method" → type "select", with select options named exactly: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting", "Self-Consistency", "Tree of Thoughts", "Process Supervision", "Automatic CoT"
  - "Key_Contribution" → type "rich_text"
  - "Cited_By" → type "number"

## Step 2 — Add one entry (database row) per paper
Use `mcp__notion__API-post-page` with parent {"type": "database_id", "database_id": "<the new database id>"} for each of the following 5 papers. Set the properties as specified.

### Entry 1
- Title: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models"
- Authors: "Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans"
- Year: 2022
- Method: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting"
- Key_Contribution: "Introduced chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting: augmenting few-shot exemplars with a series of intermediate reasoning steps so the model decomposes complex problems into simpler sub-steps. Requires no fine-tuning and is an emergent ability of sufficiently large models (~100B parameters). With PaLM 540B, GSM8K accuracy rose from 17.9% (standard prompting) to 56.9%; gains also on SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS, CommonsenseQA and StrategyQA, plus symbolic reasoning tasks."
- Cited_By: 4500

### Entry 2
- Title: "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models"
- Authors: "Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans"
- Year: 2022
- Method: "Self-Consistency"
- Key_Contribution: "Replaces greedy decoding in CoT with a sample-and-vote strategy: prompt with CoT exemplars, sample a diverse set of reasoning paths at non-zero temperature, then marginalize over the paths by majority voting on the final answer. Unsupervised, no extra training. GSM8K with PaLM 540B improved from 56.9% (CoT) to 74.4%; ARC +3.9%; gains saturate at roughly 40 sampled paths."
- Cited_By: 2600

### Entry 3
- Title: "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models"
- Authors: "Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao"
- Year: 2023
- Method: "Tree of Thoughts"
- Key_Contribution: "Generalizes CoT from a single linear path to deliberate exploration of multiple reasoning paths in a tree, enabling lookahead, alternative exploration and backtracking. The LM acts as both generator and evaluator via four components: thought decomposition, thought generation (sampling or proposal prompting), state evaluation (value or vote prompting), and BFS/DFS search. With GPT-4: Game of 24 solved 74% vs 4% for CoT; Mini Crosswords 60% vs 16% for best-of-100 CoT sampling; also improved Creative Writing as judged by GPT-4."
- Cited_By: 1500

### Entry 4
- Title: "Let's Verify Step by Step"
- Authors: "Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda"
- Year: 2023
- Method: "Process Supervision"
- Key_Contribution: "Shows that process-based reward models (PRMs), which score every individual step of a chain of thought, substantially outperform outcome-based reward models (ORMs) that only score the final answer. Human annotators labelled each step correct/incorrect/neutral, and the resulting PRM was used to verify and select among multiple candidate solutions. On MATH: 78.2% (PRM) vs 72.4% (ORM) vs 53.2% (majority voting). Also released PRM800K, a dataset of 800K step-level human feedback labels."
- Cited_By: 900

### Entry 5
- Title: "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models"
- Authors: "Zhuosheng Zhang, Aston Zhang, Mu Li"
- Year: 2022
- Method: "Automatic CoT"
- Key_Contribution: "Proposes Auto-CoT, which removes the manual effort of hand-crafting CoT exemplars. It clusters dataset questions using sentence embeddings plus k-means to sample diverse questions, then generates each demonstration's reasoning chain with zero-shot CoT ('Let's think step by step'), so the demonstrations cover diverse reasoning patterns. Across 10 reasoning benchmarks including MultiArith, GSM8K and CommonsenseQA it matches or exceeds manual CoT (e.g. MultiArith 92.0% vs 91.7%)."
- Cited_By: 600

## Notes
- Use the exact property names above, including the underscores in "Key_Contribution" and "Cited_By".
- For select properties pass e.g. {"select": {"name": "Tree of Thoughts"}}; for numbers pass {"number": 2022}; for rich_text pass {"rich_text": [{"text": {"content": "..."}}]}; for the title property pass {"title": [{"text": {"content": "..."}}]}.
- If a "Method" option does not yet exist in the select when you add a page, pass it anyway via the select name and it will normally be created; if creation fails, first use `mcp__notion__API-update-a-database` to add the missing option, then retry.

## Report back
Confirm: the created database ID and URL, the exact property schema you created, and a list of the 5 created page IDs with their titles. If anything fails, report exactly what failed and what you tried.
Create Notion Reasoning Papers DB

You are scheduling reading group sessions on the team's Google Calendar. This is an authorized write task.

## Context
Our research group is surveying reasoning methods for large language models. We reviewed 5 papers and want one one-hour reading-group session per day, Monday through Friday, in the week of March 16-20, 2026.

## Step 1 — Check for conflicts (read-only)
Use `mcp__google_calendar__list_events` with timeMin "2026-03-16T00:00:00Z" and timeMax "2026-03-21T00:00:00Z" to see what already exists in that window. Report what you find. (Do not delete anything.)

## Step 2 — Create the 5 events
Use `mcp__google_calendar__create_event` for each of the following. Times MUST be expressed as UTC. Pass start/endTime in the form "2026-03-16T10:00:00Z" (trailing Z, no separate timeZone field), e.g.:

- start: {"dateTime": "2026-03-16T10:00:00Z"}
- end: {"dateTime": "2026-03-16T11:00:00Z"}

Each event is exactly one hour, 10:00-11:00 UTC.

| # | Date | Summary (exact title) | Paper covered |
|---|------|----------------------|---------------|
| 1 | Monday 2026-03-16 | Reading Group: Chain-of-Thought | Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (Wei, Wang, Schuurmans, 2022) |
| 2 | Tuesday 2026-03-17 | Reading Group: Self-Consistency | Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, 2022) |
| 3 | Wednesday 2026-03-18 | Reading Group: Tree-of-Thought | Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (Yao, Yu, Zhao, 2023) |
| 4 | Thursday 2026-03-19 | Reading Group: Step-by-Step Verification | Let's Verify Step by Step (Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda, 2023) |
| 5 | Friday 2026-03-20 | Reading Group: Auto-CoT | Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models (Zhang, Zhang, Li, 2022) |

For each event also set a description like:
"Reading group session covering <full paper title> (<authors>, <year>). <one-sentence description of the method>."

Suggested one-sentence descriptions:
1. "Chain-of-thought prompting augments few-shot exemplars with intermediate reasoning steps, lifting GSM8K accuracy with PaLM 540B from 17.9% to 56.9%."
2. "Self-consistency samples diverse CoT reasoning paths and selects the most consistent answer by majority voting, improving GSM8K from 56.9% to 74.4% with PaLM 540B."
3. "Tree of Thoughts generalizes CoT into tree-structured search with LM-based self-evaluation, backtracking and BFS/DFS, reaching 74% on Game of 24 versus 4% for CoT."
4. "Process supervision trains a step-level reward model that verifies each step of a chain of thought, reaching 78.2% on MATH versus 72.4% for an outcome-based verifier."
5. "Auto-CoT automatically builds CoT demonstrations by clustering diverse questions and generating reasoning chains with zero-shot CoT, matching manual CoT performance."

Do NOT set attendees, recurrence, or reminders. Do NOT pass a timeZone field (the trailing Z already makes the time unambiguous UTC).

## Report back
Confirm the event IDs, titles, and exact start/end datetimes you created, plus anything you found in the conflict check. If any creation fails, report the error exactly.
